claims.text: The target nanoparticles are noble-metal HEAs synthesized from more than five single-source precursors.
Single-phase HEA nanoparticle formation and crystal-structure selection are primarily governed by inhibited precursor mobility.
Formation of low-temperature noble-metal HEA nanoparticles is governed by stochastic principles.
Rapid heating and cooling produce kinetically constrained reduction events.
Kinetically constrained reduction freezes a random elemental distribution into a single-phase alloy.
Enhanced atomic mobility permits diffusion following disparate reduction events and causes phase separation or elemental segregation.
The initial precursor mixture is homogeneous.
The baseline rapid kinetic process normally produces well-dispersed, single-phase HEA nanoparticles.
An intermediate-temperature hold or extended dwell will enhance atomic mobility relative to rapid heating and cooling.
Low-temperature synthesis can form single-phase nanoparticles from five noble-metal single-source precursors.
Restricted mobility governs nucleation and stochastic elemental incorporation.
Sequential reductions under inhibited mobility result in random elemental assembly.
The baseline nanoparticles have a uniform elemental distribution.
An extended dwell will increase phase separation, elemental segregation, or the number of crystalline phases relative to the rapid-reduction baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal systems containing at least five elements when kinetic constraints dominate thermodynamic diffusion.
The stochastic model is supported for five-element noble-metal systems.
Individual elemental reduction kinetics may alter the response to dwell time and temperature.
Failure of the enhanced-mobility condition to produce a statistically significant increase in separation, segregation, or additional phases would falsify the proposed mobility-controlled mechanism.

contradictions.description: The main target is specified as containing more than five elements, whereas the boundary includes five-element systems and the proposed experiment explicitly uses five-element nanoparticles. Thus, the experiment does not directly test the stated >5-element regime.
